title: Where should the Bill draw the line?
label: 19 November 2026 · Family law and the Bill
summary: The committee examined whether the draft Bill clearly defines harmful conversion practices and protects children without catching ordinary family conversations. FFLAG supported the Bill while proposing several changes; Matilda Gosling argued that its broad wording could restrict parents and professionals, especially when a young person is questioning their gender. Family lawyers Sarah Branson and Shabana Jaffar said the definitions should be clearer and distinguished from the established family-court test for serious harm. They also discussed protective court orders, possible misuse in parental disputes, the pressures on courts and whether children could face criminal consequences.

glossary.definition: A court order intended to prevent someone from subjecting another person to a conversion practice.
The established family-law test for serious harm that can justify state intervention to protect a child.
A court order that gives a local authority legal responsibility for a child's care.
A court order allowing a local authority to oversee and support a child and family while the child stays at home.
The High Court's power to act in cases where no specific law already provides a solution.
Changes such as a young person using a different name, pronouns or clothing to live as a different gender.
A course of medical assessment or treatment related to a person's gender.
A parenting approach that combines warmth and support with clear rules and boundaries.
Female genital mutilation: procedures that injure or alter female genital organs for non-medical reasons.
A court order designed to protect someone from being forced to marry.
Public funding that can help people pay for legal advice or representation.

chapters.title: What the Bill should cover
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses disagreed about whether the Bill's definitions are clear enough, while FFLAG supported its aim and proposed specific changes.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The committee is examining the draft Bill, which aims to prevent and criminalise harmful conversion practices. Are its definitions clear enough, especially when applied to families?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: In family court, we use a familiar test called “significant harm” to decide when the state can intervene in family life. The Bill uses different terms, and it's unclear whether its threshold is higher, lower or intended to mean the same thing.

turns.speaker: Des Johnson
turns.text: FFLAG welcomes the Bill. We support parents and families of LGBT+ people, and we believe these practices are a distinct form of abuse that isn't adequately addressed by existing laws.

turns.speaker: Des Johnson
turns.text: A 2018 national survey found that 2% of LGBT respondents had experienced conversion practices, rising to 4% among trans respondents. We don't have reliable figures for people who are agender, though families tell us they exist.

turns.speaker: Des Johnson
turns.text: We think these practices come from the belief that someone's sexual orientation or gender identity can be changed and that it's somehow wrong. Children aren't broken and don't need to be fixed.

turns.speaker: Des Johnson
turns.text: We'd add suppression as well as attempts to change someone. We'd also limit the healthcare exemption to properly regulated professionals, clarify that the Bill targets practices meeting a criminal threshold, and include conduct likely to cause serious harm.

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: I'm particularly concerned about how the Bill applies to children questioning their gender. Their situations can involve trauma, family circumstances and other factors, but the Bill risks treating gender identity and sexual orientation as equivalent.

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: Some teenagers referred to gender services were same-sex attracted. In my view, helping a gender-nonconforming young person feel comfortable in their body could be treated as an attempt to change their identity.

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: The Bill also doesn't clearly distinguish children from adults. Terms such as emotional pressure could cover ordinary parenting, and young people's identities may develop over time.

turns.speaker: Danny Beales
turns.text: You link some young people's gender identity with trauma and care experience. Are you saying that these experiences mean gender identity should be treated differently from sexual orientation?

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: I'm saying that trauma or care experience may be relevant to understanding why some young people identify as transgender. I cited research suggesting looked-after children were over-represented among young people referred to gender services.

turns.speaker: Danny Beales
turns.text: People who are gay, lesbian or bisexual can also experience trauma. And surely young people need support and open conversations, rather than practices intended to change them?

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: I agree they need support and open conversations. My concern is that the broad definition could also cover those conversations. I also think the evidence on gender identity is less measurable and stable than evidence on sexual orientation.

turns.speaker: Danny Beales
turns.text: I don't agree with that distinction. Both sexual orientation and gender identity involve identity, and people's understanding of their sexuality can also develop.

chapters.title: Parents, conversations and unintended effects
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses disputed whether the draft could chill ordinary parenting, and several called for wording that makes its limits easier to understand.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: Could parents or professionals be investigated even if they don't ultimately face a conviction?

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: I worry about complaints from relatives, teachers or other people, including during disputes between separated parents. Parents may then avoid discussing a young person's identity, and children could feel able to pressure a parent.

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: Good parenting often combines warmth with boundaries. If parents fear that setting limits could be treated as unlawful pressure, that could make family relationships more difficult.

turns.speaker: Shabana Jaffar
turns.text: At CAFCASS, we often deal with separated parents. The draft could make them afraid to have ordinary conversations about a child's views, especially if they disagree about how to respond.

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: If Parliament doesn't intend to prohibit open-ended conversations, assessment or advice that helps someone explore their experiences without pushing a particular conclusion, it should say so clearly.

turns.speaker: Lord Isaac
turns.text: The offence has several tests that all have to be met. Do you still think an ordinary conversation could realistically cross that threshold?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: My concern is also practical. Social workers may worry that a conversation with a child in care could break the law, even if a lawyer might later conclude that it didn't meet every test. Clear drafting would help them do their jobs.

turns.speaker: Des Johnson
turns.text: The Bill doesn't target normal, difficult family conversations. It requires an intention to change someone, and the serious distress test is about a substantial effect on their day-to-day life.

turns.speaker: Des Johnson
turns.text: The Bill doesn't force parents to affirm a child's identity or fund every choice. A parent could, for example, refuse to buy a binder because they're worried about its health effects without trying to change who their child is.

turns.speaker: Des Johnson
turns.text: Parenting an LGBT+ child can involve fear, uncertainty, grief and messy conversations. The Bill is aimed at the small minority who feel compelled to change a child, not those ordinary difficulties.

turns.speaker: Naz Shah
turns.text: Sarah, as the Bill is currently drafted, do you think parents risk being investigated simply for not affirming a child's identity?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: The fact that we're still debating what the wording means shows why it needs to be clearer.

turns.speaker: Marie Goldman
turns.text: Would the panel support a plain clarification in the Bill, so parents and professionals who aren't lawyers can understand what's allowed?

turns.speaker: Des Johnson
turns.text: Yes. The law should make clear that it targets attempts to change someone, and other countries' laws offer examples of ways to spell out what isn't covered.

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: A clarification would help, but I don't think it solves everything. I'd also want the Bill to address how it applies to children and young adults, whose identities may continue to develop.

turns.speaker: Baroness Browning
turns.text: Could children themselves be drawn into complaints, including in disputes between siblings?

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: Yes. Children under the age of criminal responsibility—currently 10—could potentially be affected. Siblings argue, and the Bill needs to address whether a child could be accused of an offence.

turns.speaker: Danny Beales
turns.text: Have bans in other countries actually stopped parents from having open conversations?

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: In research I conducted, some mental health professionals in places including Canada and parts of the United States described a chilling effect on their work and on parents. My research focused mainly on clinicians; I can provide the committee with the material about parents.

turns.speaker: Des Johnson
turns.text: The committee should ask countries with these laws about their experience. They have had time to gather evidence that could support or challenge those concerns.

turns.speaker: Lord Isaac
turns.text: Do you accept that abusive conversion practices happen?

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: I haven't seen evidence that establishes it, but I'm sure it happens and I agree it shouldn't. I don't know where the gap in existing law is, and some research may count conduct that isn't what people usually mean by a conversion practice.

chapters.title: What family courts can already do
chapters.takeaway: Existing family law can address serious harm, but Sarah Branson said it lacks a clear, specific way to prevent some practices before they happen.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: Is “abusive” clear enough, or would courts have to work out its meaning case by case?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: It's doing a lot of work in the Bill without being defined. In family law, “significant harm” has a well-established meaning from legislation and court decisions. I'd use that familiar test if the family courts are meant to make protective orders.

turns.speaker: Shabana Jaffar
turns.text: Family practitioners and local authorities are used to defined tests. The wording here is broad and open to interpretation, which makes it harder to know when intervention is justified.

turns.speaker: Lord Scriven
turns.text: If parents repeatedly subject a 14-year-old to religious deliverance sessions, sleep deprivation and isolation from friends, could family law deal with it now?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: Yes. If that amounted to significant harm caused by the parents' care, the court could make a care order or a supervision order. Those measures could remove a child from home or allow the local authority to supervise the family.

turns.speaker: Lord Scriven
turns.text: What if parents plan to send their 15-year-old abroad for a conversion programme?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: If the test for significant harm is met, the local authority could step in. But family law doesn't have a specific order to stop that practice before it happens. The High Court may have powers to act where there's no specific law, but there are few cases to guide us.

turns.speaker: Lord Isaac
turns.text: Could using family-law language in a Bill that also creates criminal offences confuse the two systems?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: The draft risks asking family courts to make decisions using language from criminal law that they don't normally apply. If the family court is meant to protect children from these practices, the Bill should say what test it must use.

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: My suggestion is to use conduct that causes, or is likely to cause, significant harm as the family-court test. Judges, local authorities and lawyers already understand that standard.

turns.speaker: Olivia Bailey
turns.text: If some harmful conduct is already covered by other offences, is there still value in naming conversion practices in law?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: There can be. Naming a practice can help professionals recognise it, and a specific law can allow courts to make preventive orders instead of waiting for an offence to happen. That's how other protective laws can work, including those concerning forced marriage and FGM.

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Silvertown
turns.text: Have parents faced action for conversion practices? And could the law apply when the young person is 16, 17 or 18?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: I found very few reported cases on conversion practices specifically. Courts can address emotional harm when it meets the required threshold, and I've seen a reported case where a court made an order after a mother imposed her belief that her son was transgender.

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: Care and supervision orders can be made until a young person is 17. After that, the High Court or, in more limited situations, the Court of Protection may have powers.

turns.speaker: Shabana Jaffar
turns.text: In my own practice, I haven't seen a case where the local authority couldn't use its existing powers to protect a child.

chapters.title: Protection orders and family disputes
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses saw value in preventive orders but warned that the application process, court powers and appeal rules need clearer limits.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: Could parents use a protection-order application to involve a child in a dispute with the other parent?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: The Bill says certain people can apply, and others can apply if the court gives permission. I'd reverse the emphasis: no one should be able to apply unless the court first gives permission. That would make the court examine why the application is being made.

turns.speaker: Shabana Jaffar
turns.text: I share that concern. Parents already have to navigate a complicated court system, and a new type of order could become another way of drawing a child into a parental dispute.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: Should the Bill give a fixed list of things the court can order, such as stopping foreign travel?

turns.speaker: Shabana Jaffar
turns.text: The court could also have power to make other provisions it considers necessary. Courts can develop how orders work through decisions in later cases.

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: These orders can be complex, so I think full-time judges should deal with them. The Bill doesn't say clearly which level of judge would hear the cases.

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: Preventive orders can sometimes help keep a child with their family. Without a less restrictive option, the choice may be between doing nothing and removing the child into foster care.

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: An order could, for example, prevent a child being taken abroad or stop a harmful practice. If a family would follow the order, it might protect the child without separating them from their parents.

turns.speaker: Shabana Jaffar
turns.text: Orders stopping travel are often temporary while the court works out the level of risk. Long-running restrictions can cause problems for families, so courts may need to review them.

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: Restrictions should be necessary and proportionate. I'm also unclear about the Bill's appeal rules: it appears to let someone who wasn't part of the case appeal, but doesn't explain who can do that or when.

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: Unlike orders addressing a specific act such as FGM, these orders could concern a broad range of actions linked to gender identity. The Bill doesn't clearly limit what a court could require, and a parent might be required to support social transition or pay for items they don't agree with.

chapters.title: Effects on courts, services and children
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses said the family justice system is already stretched and called for resources and clarity about how the Bill applies to children.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What would the Bill mean for family courts and services for young people?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: Courts and legal professionals are already under pressure. Private family cases can wait a year or more for a final hearing, and lawyers doing publicly funded work haven't had an inflation-linked pay rise for many years. If the Bill creates more work, the system needs the resources to handle it.

turns.speaker: Shabana Jaffar
turns.text: Family services are also managing other reforms. Local authorities already handle more private family cases under a new child-focused court process, and the Bill could lead to more safeguarding referrals. We can't say how many, but that possibility needs consideration.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Bill applies to children as well as adults. Could a child be treated as having committed an offence by trying to change someone else?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: The age of criminal responsibility is 10. Parliament needs to decide whether children that young are intended to face criminal consequences under this Bill. If not, the law should say so.

turns.speaker: Shabana Jaffar
turns.text: The draft doesn't explain what would happen to a child in that situation, and that's a concern.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: Should the Bill spell out what parents and other adults can do, so they don't misunderstand it?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: Yes. If lawyers are still debating what the wording means, parents and professionals need clearer guidance in the law itself.

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: That clarity should cover other adults involved in a child's life too, including teachers, social workers and relatives.
